items.title: Why Pond ditched psych rock for new 'Goths at the pub' style
paras: After 10 albums of revered psych rock, WA band Pond rewired their sound but not their subject matter. ( Supplied: Sam Kristofski )
Emerging in 2008 from the same Perth scene that birthed Tame Impala (the same suburban share house, in fact), Pond have long been at the vanguard of modern psychedelic rock and pop.
On their 11th album, however, the West Australian five-piece laid down some ground rules.
Denying themselves their lysergic signifiers came out of a simple desire for change and "have something to think about and reach for," frontman Nick Allbrook tells Double J's Michael Hing .
"Instead of 'should we do another Pond album?' Because that's a mind-numbingly boring idea."
Instead, the group "hatched this plan of making a short, sharp, angular" album and devised a new style guide — "Goths at the pub."
The resulting album, Terrestrials, bridges distinctive 1980s aesthetics: sunburnt, acid-washed Oz rock and moody, largely British post-punk.
Think Icehouse, The Church and Sisters of Mercy sharing a bill in the back room.
Compared to Pond's last album, 2024's sprawling, career-overview Stung! , Terrestrials is leaner and more cohesive.
The riffs and rhythms are more urgent; the pounding drums avoid cymbals while synths dispense spaciness for taut clarity.
Recording live to tape together in the room also gifts the album a closeness and cleanliness without sacrificing their heaviness or energy.
For a band historically described as psychedelic cosmonauts, there is a gritty presence to Terrestrials, which — as its title underscores — finds inspiration in very earthly concerns.
Allbrook has spent most of his career meditating on Australia's national identity. More specifically, chronicling the conflict between Western Australian commerce and culture.
Stripping away Pond's trippy signatures for something more sinewy only makes his lyrical plights and political barbs more pointed.
Contemplating Australia Day's history and the titular City of Perth fireworks celebrations that accompany it, angular opener Skyworks comes over like modern-day Midnight Oil.

Ditto the thumping Casuarina, which critiques the "ongoing institutional neglect and violence" at the titular WA high-security prison that led to the death in custody of 16-year-old Cleveland Dodd at the "inhumane" Unit 18 .
Meanwhile, the scrappy, scathing Two Hands laments Rio Tinto's destruction of Juukun Gorge — a 47,000-year-old sacred site for local First Nations communities — with its rallying chorus:
"If your blood pumps and your heart beats / I'll meet you on the corner of my street / And our two hands can make a fist / Red mist."
"You're inspired to write about the things that loom largest in your mind," notes Allbrook.
"I'm not necessarily thinking 'Right, I'm going to build a great body of work about Western Australia and its people.'"
But he is fascinated with what he calls "the sunburnt, blistered, debauched freaks" on the fringes of WA culture.
"The fear, anxiety, horror, innate goodness, hope — all this stuff that resides within those people … I'm writing about myself really. And my family and my home."
Born in Fremantle, Allbrook spent his childhood in the remote town of Derby in the Kimberley region before returning to Perth as a high-schooler.
Part of the city's burgeoning 2000s grassroots scene, Allbrook found local infamy fronting Mink Mussel Creek, one of several bands comprising the same line-up of like-minded muso friends.

That included drummer Kevin Parker, who would later achieve award-hoovering global acclaim as Tame Impala. Allbrook and Jay "GUM" Watson, who were then Tame touring members, teamed with "Shiny" Joe Ryan to form Pond in 2008.
They went from being a weirder, wilder offshoot to an internationally touring band with breakout 2013 record Beard, Wives, Denim (produced by Parker, who still occasionally joins his mate on tour ).
They solidified their line-up over the next decade, with keyboardist Jamie Terry and drummer James Ireland, and their clout for consistently well-received records and live shows.
Allbrook performing at the 2017 Splendour In The Grass festival. ( triple j: Lauren Connelly )
Allbrook developed a manic stage presence, but the unhinged goblin persona he cultivated belies the progressive, deep thinker of his poetic lyrics and solo records.
He is fascinated with the "brokenness and beauty" of Western Australia, unafraid to interrogate how it has benefited from a history of colonialism, genocide and resource extraction.
"It's embarrassing," he says. "The state capture by mining oligarchs like Gina Rinehart and Twiggy [Andrew Forrest] guides everything."
Or corporations like Woodside Energy sponsoring WA arts events and "my beloved Freo Dockers," he continues.
"Grubby fingers are in everything we do. Even the most well-meaning people, like our Premier Roger Cook; no-one's immune from the glittering prizes they offer."
Terrestrials reckons with humanity's greed and hell-bent instinct for destroying our landscapes.
Named for a stretch of wetland east of Broome, the jangling Roebuck Plains is sung from the perspective of a miner questioning his livelihood.
"When it gets dry, I feel like I'm dying in Tom Price," Allbrook sings, name-checking the iron ore mining town owned and operated by Rio Tinto.
The driving title track confronts anxieties around "unborn tomorrows and dead yesterdays" with a quintessential Australian refrain: "She'll be alright."
It speaks to the optimism that hums beneath these kinetic, rust-coloured songs concerning ecological collapse, state corruption and humanity's tendency for self-destruction.
"I recently realised that when I'm really strung out, stressed, sad … the most immediate antidote to that is rockin' out!
After touring Terrestrials in the US, next month, Pond kick off a homecoming run of theatre shows, bringing a little energy and empathy to folks with their artful racket.
As Allbrook poetically surmises, "we're an ugly bunch, but we've got great wells of love and hope in us."
Pond kicks off their headline tour in Fremantle on December 5, before playing Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney.

items.title: Is 'old person smell' real? How social media harnesses shame for sales
paras: Claims abound online about the chemical 2-nonenal being responsible for an "aged" body odour. ( Unsplash: Simon Godfrey )

Radio National's What's That Rash? received several emails from listeners who were concerned about "old person smell" after seeing ads for persimmon soap in their social media feeds. Here's one of the emails:
I have been seeing so many posts on Instagram about persimmon soap that is marketed as getting rid of "old person smell".

According to the marketing, as we age we excrete an oil that has an odour that permeates our clothes and houses that apparently the old person cannot smell but everyone else can. Even if we wash our body and clothes daily it won't get rid of the odour except if you use persimmon soap.
As I am over 70 and do wash my body daily and launder clothes regularly, I am very worried I might be a smelly old lady without knowing it!
Is there any truth in this, and if there is, is there any scientific evidence that using persimmon soap works?
We looked at the (small amount of) research, and spoke to experts. Here's what we found:
According to advertisers and some researchers, "old person smell" is caused by a chemical called 2-nonenal.
Deshan Sebaratnam, a dermatologist at The Skin Hospital in Sydney, says many different variables can contribute to someone's smell.
"The bacteria on their skin, the composition of their oil and sweat, hormones, diet, hygiene practices [and] genetics," Dr Sebaratnam says.
"There is some evidence that 2-nonenal may contribute, but it is based on a small group of people."
The claim originated from a 2001 study of 22 Japanese people that found 2-nonenal was only present in men aged 40 and over.
Another Japanese study in 2016 , this time with 27 participants using a different measurement, also found 2-nonenal increased with age.
Another small study in the US in 2009 , was unable to detect the chemical in men or women over 39.
The authors concluded that 2-nonenal "might be a diet-linked, cultural phenomenon, which may not generalise to non-Japanese populations".
"The large consumption of fish and marine-based foods in the Japanese diet may lead to a build-up of unsaturated fatty acids and lipid peroxides with aging," they wrote.
While evidence for 2-nonenal is shaky, another small study suggests humans can accurately guess a person's age based on smell alone.
Body odour "donors" wore T-shirts with armpit pads for five nights before they were presented to the study's sniffers.
While the sniffers could identify older donors, they rated their smell as less intense and less unpleasant than younger donors.
Online sites sell the orange-coloured soap for up to $72 for a single bar.
These ads declare their "clinically proven" and "doctor-backed" soaps don't just cover up the supposed smell, but neutralise or even eliminate 2-nonenal.
"I have reservations about there being anything particularly special about persimmon soap," Dr Sebaratnam says.
Advertisers claim their persimmon soaps can "neutralise" 2-nonenal. ( Unsplash: Eden )
In 2012, researchers tested a soap containing persimmon, oolong, sweet and green tea extracts on a small group of middle-aged Japanese men concerned about their smell.
After using the soap for four weeks, participants and "odour judges" said participants smelled nicer, researchers reported in the niche Journal of the Japanese Odor and Fragrance Environment .
But the researchers didn't compare the persimmon blend to any other soap.
That means there's no way to know whether this subjective change in smell was due to the persimmon, the tea, or more thorough washing brought on by the pressures of the study.
Giselle Newton, a digital sociologist at the University of Queensland who tracks advertisements for the Australian Ad Observatory, has noticed a clear pattern in health and hygiene ads.
"We see messages of urgency, encouraging consumers to take care of themselves in particular ways," Dr Newton says.
"When all of a sudden there's panic around particular people smelling a particular way, it encourages them to buy different products."
A single bar of persimmon soap can set you back anywhere between $8 and $72. ( Getty Images: Smith Collection/Gado )

Ads for persimmon soaps marketed online to older people for "age-related body odour" or kareishū use words such as "feel close to the ones you love again", "smell normal", "feel like yourself again" and "your family will notice the difference."
While these tactics have been used for years on billboards, television and websites, Dr Newton says using personal data to target people on social media takes this to another level.
"If advertisers are, to a certain extent, fabricating problems with people's bodies, then they should be held accountable for that.

items.title: Leaked webinar reveals cult leader's 'unscrupulous' reincarnation scam
paras: Universal Medicine founder Serge Benhayon was found by a court to prey on cancer patients. ( Supplied )
A leaked webinar reveals how an Australian healing cult that has harvested millions from dying followers is coaching members to avoid legal challenges to their wills from family.
The Background Briefing podcast has uncovered shocking new details of the reincarnation scam run by Universal Medicine, which was found by a court to be an "exploitative" cult.

Cult leader Serge Benhayon, 62, claims he is the reincarnation of historical luminaries including Leonardo da Vinci, and indoctrinates members on how to ascend in their "next life". Critics say his dictates control everything from members' diets to their sex lives.

The bankrupt tennis coach turned multimillionaire guru has built an occult healing empire selling bogus therapies including "esoteric breast massage" and "ovarian readings", boasting about 1,000 followers worldwide, including doctors, executives, directors and academics.
A slide from the leaked Universal Medicine webinar lays out Serge Benhayon's reincarnation premise. ( Supplied )
Mr Benhayon has told followers that "if you are leaving an inheritance to your children, the way they spend the money affects you in your next life".
"Anyone that leaves money to Universal Medicine, we will know how to best use it."
The Universal Medicine webinar recording obtained by the Background Briefing podcast reveals a systematic harvesting of bequests from cult followers.

In the session conducted in October 2025, senior cult member Heather Pope lectured followers about preparing their estates to minimise the workload for cult beneficiaries, including the Benhayon family.
Universal Medicine's Heather Pope complained about how a deceased member's estate was left. ( Supplied: A Case of the Livingness )

Ms Pope, whose LinkedIn profile describes her as a senior manager in the multinational corporation NTT, said it was "not up to Serge or any Benhayon … to take care of the physical … aspects of our passing over".
In the webinar slides, Ms Pope scored deceased followers out of 10 for how they'd prepared their estates in the categories of "legals", "belongings" and "financials".

One follower who recently died of cancer scored only "five out of ten" in legal matters because they "hadn't really advised their family" that they would be leaving money to the cult, paving the way for a legal challenge.
Ms Pope also complained that the follower's car and jewellery were tied up in probate: "If you sign it over beforehand, that makes it so much simpler for your beneficiary," she said.
According to former cult member Brendan Jones, the beneficiary in the case being described was Mr Benhayon's daughter Natalie, who owns a house and lives with Ms Pope.
Serge Benhayon's daughter, Natalie, has received substantial bequests from now deceased cult members. ( YouTube: Unimed Living )
According to Mr Jones, the car was a Porsche, which Ms Pope complained "had a flat battery" and was "so dirty I didn't want to step into it".
"I don't know if you guys are beginning to realise the inconvenience of this … is that horrifying to you?" she asked the webinar participants.
"Just say five, six, seven people all leave a car that needs taking care of … I'm just saying."
Ms Pope gave the deceased follower a score of "two out of 10" for "belongings", saying that along with the "dirty car", their clothing "was grubby, wasn't folded, had pilling on it".
In the leaked webinar, Heather Pope used colour coding to grade how former followers had prepared for their deaths. ( Supplied )
While followers had "the incredible support of Serge Benhayon with the energetics of our passing", it was up to them "to take care of everything else", Ms Pope said.
She asked the group if they could name a single follower who had "passed over and didn't have drama" and said they could "write a book about our difficulties with parents" during estate proceedings.
The "passover planning" webinar took place despite a 2018 court judgment that Mr Benhayon "swindles cancer patients" for bequests, using "fraudulent ideas of karma".
Just four months after the damning defamation judgment, the cult posted an interview to YouTube with another dying follower, Susan Evans.
"I'm leaving money to Universal Medicine because what gets done in the community by Universal Medicine is absolutely astounding," she said in the video.
Ms Evans said she had received free treatments from the cult, including "chakra puncture" during chemotherapy for her lung cancer.
Asked by the cult's PR representative if she "ever felt pressure from anyone at Universal Medicine … in terms of your will or leaving money", Ms Evans replied: "Absolutely not … not a chance."
Ms Evans, who was single with no children, died last year leaving $30,000 to a nephew and almost $670,000 in cash and assets to Mr Benhayon's daughter, Natalie.
Her brother, Michael Evans, tells Background Briefing he learned Susan was in the cult when she was diagnosed with cancer about a decade earlier.
"She said, 'I'm going to be OK because Serge [Benhayon] is going to hold me'," he says.
"I thought it was unusual that this person said they could hold her and that she was relying so much on them at this stage."
Michael Evans learnt his sister was in a cult during her cancer diagnosis. ( ABC News: Jake Grant )
Mr Evans says his sister dismissed the 2018 court findings against Mr Benhayon as "lies", saying, "No-one understands Serge".
Leaked messages from the cult's online forum show Ms Evans signed her posts "in devotion" and praised the cult leader, saying in 2022 that "with Serge Benhayon the walls come tumbling down".
After his sister's death, Mr Evans contacted a solicitor associated with the cult who informed the family "there was a will and it's all been taken care of".
A collage of images from Susan's life was displayed at her funeral. ( Supplied )
The will granted the cult's sometime lawyer and esoteric breast masseuse Serryn O'Regan control over Ms Evans' affairs, including her social media accounts.
"I feel like [Universal Medicine] had a very strong influence on her in how she dealt with her life — and also with end-of-life," Mr Evans says.
The family could not afford to challenge the will in court and were not after the money themselves, he says, but were concerned it had landed with a "socially harmful cult".
"All Susan's work is now going to help fuel an organisation that the court has found is being run by a charlatan," Mr Evans says.
Serryn O'Regan and Serge Benhayon did not respond to questions from Background Briefing.
Michael Evans says Universal Medicine influenced his sister's approach to her death. ( ABC News: Jake Grant )
Just how Mr Benhayon grooms dying patients has been revealed as long-term member Mr Jones speaks exclusively with Background Briefing's The Unbreakable Cult series.
He says the community "rallied around" Melbourne woman Camilla Allen, who moved to Byron Bay with a terminal cancer diagnosis to live with two sisters who were part of the cult.
Mr Benhayon told followers Ms Allen was "Arjuna", his long-lost sister from a past life thousands of years ago, giving her celebrity status in the group.
The founder of Universal Medicine, Serge Benhayon, was found by a court to "swindle cancer patients". ( Facebook: Serge Benhayon )
"She was so special, people wanted to go and see her," Mr Jones recalls.
"My wife at the time wanted to go and see her, 'because she's Arjuna and Serge's sister and it'd be phenomenal'."
Mr Jones says the cult leader gave Ms Allen "special attention", telling followers the cancer was "clearing" bad energy from her body.
She died in November 2022, aged 67, leaving everything to one of the sisters and fellow cult members she was living with, clinical psychologist Aimee Jeffreys.
The decision shocked her parents, who had paid for their daughter's Melbourne townhouse and a life insurance policy.
Ms Allen's brothers and childhood friends believe the cult's influence alienated Ms Allen from her family.
Serge Benhayon posted a photo of himself with Camilla Allen (centre) and Jessica and Aimee Jeffreys. ( Supplied )
The Unbreakable Cult series has obtained a recording of Mr Benhayon telling followers Ms Allen had "denounced her evil family, brothers, mum, father".
"Her first choice was to leave the country and die somewhere where her parents could not reach her — that's how much she detested her parents," he said.
"Now, because of COVID, she couldn't leave the country. She got her second option, which was the glory of being with … Aimee and myself."
A leaked text shows Mr Benhayon requesting a Zoom meeting with her beneficiary, Aimee Jeffreys, to prepare for "shenanigans" following Ms Allen's death.
Ms Allen's brothers appealed to Ms Jeffreys to return the estate to their parents, who had financed the life insurance policy and Melbourne townhouse.
Ultimately, Ms Jeffreys sold the property she inherited back to Ms Allen's parents for $250,000.
Background Briefing understands she shared some of the proceeds from Ms Allen's life insurance policies with her family.
Two years later, Aimee and her sister Jessica bought a $3 million acreage property in NSW from Mr Benhayon's wife, Miranda.
Aimee and Jessica Jeffreys and Miranda Benhayon did not respond to questions from Background Briefing.
Serge Benhayon's wife Miranda (left) and daughter Natalie (right) are prominent members of Universal Medicine. ( Supplied: Unimed living )
Senior barrister Tom Molomby represented blogger Esther Rockett in the defamation case brought by Mr Benhayon that ultimately found he was a "charlatan".
Mr Molomby proved in court that Mr Benhayon preyed on "cancer patients by targeting them to leave him bequests in their wills".
The court found Mr Benhayon "exercised undue influence" on a follower to receive $1.4 million from her estate.
The Benhayon family have purchased $25 million worth of luxury property in the Gold Coast region. ( ABC News: David Stuart )
Mr Molomby tells The Unbreakable Cult series that the judgment has set a legal precedent for a court to overturn wills set to enrich Universal Medicine.
"We proved that Benhayon had told his followers that if they wanted a good time in the next life, they should leave their money to him," he says.
"If he knew that was a lie … and that was the case I made … I call that undue influence, and I think you'd easily win it."
Mr Molomby says dying people "in thrall to the cult's crazy beliefs" were signing over their fortunes "on the basis of a complete fantasy which was benefiting" Mr Benhayon.
"They're harvesting bequests, it's not just individual cases anymore," he says.
"It's industrialised fraud, and I think it's wide open for somebody to have a go."
The blogger Mr Molomby represented, Esther Rockett, says attention should be paid to Mr Benhayon's "enablers".
Blogger Esther Rockett was sued for defamation by cult leader Serge Benhayon and won. ( ABC News: Chris Gillette )
Ms Rockett says these "very capable" assistants included lawyers, financial planners and doctors, "professional people who will do his bidding for him and bring in that money".
"It's kind of brilliant in its own way. It's just utterly unscrupulous," she says.

items.title: Albanese can stare down Putin, but can't escape reality of Trump's world
paras: President Donald Trump talks with Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, look on. ( AP: Mark Schiefelbein )
Standing in a room with Donald Trump is an exercise in understanding the gravitational pull of the American presidency.

The 80-year-old had just spent more than 18 hours travelling, but barely an hour after landing in Manila, here he was, commanding the attention of three fellow world leaders and an international press pack.

Those journalists, this column among them, had just spent the better part of three hours being ushered through security checks and shuffled around the cavernous interior of a gleaming hotel that had been entirely booked out by the White House delegation.
Anthony Albanese was in China for APEC, where he met several world leaders, including US President Donald Trump and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. ( ABC: Ian Cutmore )
Past the eerily quiet slot machines and 4.5m Christmas trees decorating the hotel's casino, the press pool was marshalled to a makeshift US security screening station next to a Prada store.

Laptop bags, cameras and sound equipment were deposited in a line on the polished floor to be searched by sniffer dogs, while a no-nonsense secret service agent shouted instructions to "maintain the integrity of the sweep".
All this just to be in the room as the Quad leaders — Trump, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Japan's Sanae Takaichi and India's Narendra Modi — delivered their scripted opening remarks.
Strict security is standard for any international summit, but to enter the orbit of Trump requires a whole new level.
He may be considered a lame duck president at home following the Republicans' catastrophic midterm election results, but diminished on the world stage he is not.
Within days, Trump would be sitting down with two other powerful men — Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, for an unprecedented trilateral meeting.
The meeting was unprecedented, undeniably historic and increasingly talked about as the most anticipated summit of the year. ( Reuters: Win McNamee/Pool )

The stakes of the Quad were low by comparison, but it was still significant that Trump had agreed to a leader-level gathering of the group Beijing believes is designed to thwart its rise in the region.
That's why the Australian media pool had war-gamed potential questions to throw at the US president should the opportunity present itself.

As it transpired, preparation was for naught — the White House journalists had already seized on the opportunity to quiz Trump while the four Quad leaders had posed for a photograph before entering the formal meeting room.
Anthony Albanese and Xi Jinping meet at APEC. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

A live stream showed Albanese and Takaichi standing politely, if not a little awkwardly, while a relaxed Trump tossed a few answers to the press on everything from the Deutsche Bank tax records leak to the saga engulfing ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang.

Modi, who could probably count on one hand the number of times he's taken a journalist's question in his 12 years in power, was the only one visibly uncomfortable and at one point gestured to suggest they all get off the stage.
He only resigned himself to the spectacle when Trump turned and described him as "a very tough man".
Clearly enjoying himself, the US President then added that Sanae was perhaps "even tougher", before he looked back at Albanese to insist "we're OK too," and slapped the Australian PM on the back.
It was a notable demonstration of collegiality given just last year Albanese's lack of rapport with Trump was exploited as a potential diplomatic weakness by the Coalition during the election.
While there's no suggestion Albanese and Trump are about to go play a round of golf any time soon, the US leader repeatedly expressed warmth toward Australia.
But the fact Trump's every aside and gesture was so closely watched served as a reminder of how much the world's diplomacy revolves around one man.

Some of the biggest challenges confronting Australia and its neighbours are being driven by decisions made in Washington, whether the war in Iran or Trump's approach to Russia and questionable commitment to defending Ukraine.
Just a few kilometres away in the trendy, somewhat gentrified end of Poblacion in Manila, cocktail bars and karaoke joints sat conspicuously empty.
Perhaps it was because the ASEAN summit was designated a citywide public holiday, but as one local explained to this column, many Manila residents "don't go out as much these days".
In the nine months since the US began bombing Tehran, the price of petrol in the Philippines surged initially by 50 per cent and remains higher than pre-war levels.

The fallout from the Middle East conflict, along with Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine, were a central through-line in Albanese's diplomatic efforts across his 11 days abroad for the summit season.
Xi Jinping attended a meeting with Anthony Albanese in Shenzen, China. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

By the time Trump, Xi and Putin met on the sidelines of APEC in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the two conflicts dominating the international stage were firmly on the agenda for talks among the three leaders with arguably the greatest capacity to influence their course.
But for all the diplomatic theatre, the resulting declaration from their unprecedented meeting delivered little in the way of concrete solutions.

At a summit supposedly devoted to regional economic cooperation, three great powers took centre stage effectively deciding among themselves who gets to shape the international order and whose interests are left out.
For Albanese, those questions go to the heart of his government's approach to foreign policy.
Australia is a middle power deeply dependent on international trade, committed to the US alliance and highly conscious of the economic and strategic weight of China.
Therefore its interests are best served by a world where countries follow agreed rules, rather than one where the strongest nations simply dictate terms.
But recent global shocks have exposed just how fragile that ambition always was.
In January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney electrified the World Economic Forum in Davos with a warning that the old international order was not coming back.
His message to middle powers was that they needed to work together or risk being pushed around by the world's biggest players.
The challenge there was whether countries like Australia, with its security tied to the US and economic prosperity closely linked to China, could ever exercise any meaningful influence.
Against that backdrop, Albanese delivered one of APEC's more pointed interventions, directly challenging Putin over his invasion of Ukraine while Trump and Xi watched on.
It was an unusual confrontation in a forum where leaders typically stick to the diplomatic language of economic cooperation.
Albanese had not known for sure that Putin would be in the room when he gave the speech but had prepared for the possibility.
Looking directly at the Russian leader, he urged him to end the war "now".
Putin did not look up, though sources present said there was a palpable shift in the room as Albanese delivered the line.
But speaking truth to power does not necessarily persuade the powerful to listen.
Albanese is not alone navigating a world where Trump, Xi and Putin make all the biggest decisions.
After almost a year of renewed enthusiasm for middle powers working together, it's not evident Australia, Canada, Europe or others have actually gained more influence.
One source familiar with this week's Quad discussion told this column Trump's comments on Ukraine did little to inspire confidence in his position.
There is no doubt Albanese has become more comfortable navigating the competing demands of Australia's relationships with Beijing and Washington.
This week he maintained the goodwill of Trump, challenged Putin to his face and was described by Xi as a bit of a "China hand" for his frequent visits to the country.
But none of those achievements automatically translate into greater influence over the decisions that matter most.
The Quad could continue to be an important vehicle for regional cooperation, but its future still depends heavily on the willingness of an unpredictable American president to engage.
Australia's economic relationship with China remains vulnerable to geopolitical tensions, and its calls for an end to the wars in Ukraine and Iran have so far done little to alter their course.
For all Albanese's diplomatic efforts, the emerging world order still looks more like one Australia is learning to navigate than one it is helping to shape.

items.title: Reserve Bank issues Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations
paras: The Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 were superseded by the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, which were issued on January 13, 2026 , and became effective from October 01, 2026. The new regulations are principle based; intended to promote ease of doing business, especially for small exporters and importers; and empower Authorised Dealers to provide quicker and more efficient service to their customers. Based on subsequent feedback received from stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has issued Amendment Regulations to Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 that were notified on November 02, 2026 , and came into effect, retrospectively, from October 01, 2026 . In this regard, to facilitate better understanding of the new trade regulations by the exporters/importers and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has placed a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 on its website. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1531

items.title: RBI imposes monetary penalty on Fusion Finance Limited
paras: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 17, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹7.50 lakh (Rupees Seven Lakh Fifty Thousand only) on Fusion Finance Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of directions issued by RBI on ‘Know Your Customer (KYC)’ and ‘Internal Ombudsman’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under section 58G(1)(b) read with section 58B(5)(aa) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its financial position as on March 31, 2026. Based on the supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for failure to comply with the RBI directions. After considering the company's reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: The company failed to obtain PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form 60 from customers, while establishing an account-based relationship with those customers; and, The company failed to escalate the partly or wholly rejected complaints to the Internal Ombudsman for a final decision within the prescribed time. This action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of this monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1537

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "C-295 facility represents work culture of New India," says PM Modi as he and Spanish PM inaugurate facility
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Vadodara (Gujarat) [ India ], October 28 (ANI): Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday inaugurated the TATA- Airbus aircraft assembly facility complex in Vadodara. The facility will manufacture C-295 aircraft at the TATA Advanced Systems Limited campus. PM Modi said that the C-295 facility represents the work culture of a new India . "Recently, we lost the country's great son Ratan Tata ji. If he had been among us today, he would have been happy, but wherever his soul is, he would be happy. This C-295 aircraft factory reflects the new work culture of New India ... When I was the Gujarat CM, it was decided to set up a factory in Vadodara to build train coaches. The factory was also prepared for production within a record time. Today, we are exporting the metro coaches manufactured in that factory to other countries. I am confident that in the future, the aircraft made in this factory will also be exported to other countries," PM Modi said. "Today the defence manufacturing ecosystem in India is touching new heights. If we had not taken concrete steps 10 years ago, it would have been impossible to reach this level today. At that time, no one could even imagine that there could be such large-scale defence manufacturing in India . But we decided to walk on the new path, set a new goal for ourselves. And today the result is before us," PM Modi added. The Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez underlined the importance of the new industrial site. Sanchez said, "Today we are not only officially inaugurating a cutting-edge industrial facility. Today we're also witnessing how an extraordinary project between two emblematic companies becomes a reality. Prime Minister Modi, this is another triumph of your vision. Your vision is to turn India into an industrial powerhouse and a magnet for investment and business. This partnership between Airbus and Tata will contribute to the progress of the India n aerospace industry and will open new doors for the arrival of other European companies." " Tata is probably the best exponent of India n industrial strength. Its products and services are present in virtually every country on the planet. Tata is a giant among giants. As for Airbus , it embodies the very essence of a united Europe. Committed to technological innovation and the creation of jobs and prosperity. For my country, for Spain , being an integral part of the Airbus consortium, defending the values it represents. Values on which the very idea of Europe is based on cooperation, modernity and progress," Sanchez added. During the inauguration of the TATA Aircraft Complex for manufacturing C-295 aircraft, Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran announced the facility's goals. "The final aircraft assembly complex for the first aircraft to be delivered is being set up here. I must commit to our Prime Minister that exactly two years from now we will deliver the first indigenously manufactured aircraft and we will request and we'll work with your office to block the date so that you can come and inaugurate the facility and receive the first product. The first 200 engineers from Tata Group are already in Spain going through the training that is required, and we have worked with 40 SME companies and we will be adding more companies to build the entire localisation that is required for the product," he said. This collaboration between Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL) and Airbus Spain will mark India 's first private sector final assembly line (FAL) for military aircraft, boosting the nation's aerospace capabilities. The plant, located at TASL's Vadodara campus, is part of India 's Rs 2.5 billion deal signed in 2021 to acquire 56 C-295 military transport aircraft from Airbus . Under the agreement, Airbus will deliver 16 aircraft directly from Spain , while the remaining 40 will be manufactured in India by TASL. This project will create a comprehensive ecosystem for aircraft development, covering assembly, testing, certification, and maintenance throughout the lifecycle of the aircraft. Major India n defence players like Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL) and Bharat Dynamics Ltd (BDL), along with smaller enterprises, are also contributing to this project. The C-295 aircraft will strengthen India 's Air Force fleet with a modern and more reliable transport solution. Earlier in the day, PM Modi and Sanchez participated in a roadshow in Vadodara as they headed to inaugurate Tata Advanced Systems Ltd's facility. (ANI)

items.title: India is the top market for investment globally: Mark Mobius
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Mark Mobius, Founder of Mobius Capital Partners LLP , and an ace investor with expertise in emerging markets said, India's is the top stock market globally where he would like to invest. In an exclusive interview with ANI, the octagenarian said, "India would have to come first when I think about investment," Mobius stated, "Of course, India would have to be the first choice. Then, I would probably look at Taiwan. It's a Chinese society, but it's a free society and they're doing very well. Now we're beginning to see China rise again. There will be some interesting companies in China, but still, India remains our top pick." Mobius highlighted technology as his favorite sector to invest in India. "In the future, I believe there's going to be significant growth in hardware technology. As you know, India is already strong in software technology, but moving forward, hardware manufacturing will gain momentum here in India," he said. Discussing India's semiconductor infrastructure, Mobius mentioned that it is already developing. "Many of the world's large semiconductor companies already have software development operations in India, employing thousands of software engineers. The next step, of course, is hardware. Soon, we'll see large semiconductor manufacturing plants. The scale of investment we're talking about isn't in the millions, but billions of dollars, to produce the most advanced semiconductors in the world." Mobius also fondly remembered Ratan Tata, who passed away this month. "I met him many years ago and found him to be a very friendly, humble, and insightful person. I was deeply saddened to hear about his passing. I considered him one of the great Indian entrepreneurs of the century," Mobius added. Earlier on Monday, Mark Mobius, speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2024, reiterated he was bullish on India's real estate and semiconductor sectors, as he outlined the potential of these two key industries. In the semiconductor space, he said fabrication companies (fabs) will come here because India has got the population and the labour force. The octagenarian believes India will become "the leader" of the semiconductor industry. The government has so far approved five semiconductor units in India, of which construction in two sites is on, and soon the work in the other three will start. The companies have already made a cumulative investment of almost Rs 1.5 lakh crore. While talking about the parameters he looks at while investing in companies, Mobius said he looks at the growth of earnings in companies, along with the return on capital invested, and the quality of management. Asked about his investment advice to his "younger self," Mobius said, "Don't be in a rush, and study carefully". He added that one has to listen to the market. (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry. (ADVERTORIAL DISCLAIMER: The above press release has been provided by VMPL . ANI will not be responsible in any way for the content of the same)

items.title: Jannik Sinner told he won’t be able to copy Novak Djokovic’s ‘miraculous’ injury comeback if he has knee surgery
paras: Jannik Sinner has been absent from the tennis tour for four months now, ever since he beat Alexander Zverev to lift the Wimbledon title. Ironically, it is the German who has since taken advantage of this subsequent power vacuum, winning a second Grand Slam title whilst also ascending to world number one.

At the beginning, it felt like the Italian’s decision to withdraw from Canada, and later Cincinnati, was merely precautionary. However, it’s since become clear that something far more sinister was at play, with that same knee injury now persisting deep into November.

Is Daniil Medvedev the best player in the world other than Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner now? If not, who do you consider to be ahead of him? Sinner has been warned about his fitness and the long-term damage this particular issue could have on his career.
items.impact: The American spoke in response to a question which looked ahead to the Australian Open.

items.title: Ben Shelton Shuts Down 2026 Season With Mixed Feelings
paras: Ben Shelton admits there have been periods of the season when he failed to perform at his desired level, despite achieving a series of firsts in his career. The 24-year-old contested his first Grand Slam final in September at the US Open, where he was beaten in four sets by Alexander Zverev.

Shelton has also successfully defended his title at the Canadian Masters, as well as winning two ATP 500s and one 250 since January. Earlier this month, he was runner-up at the Paris Masters to Carlos Alcaraz.

Shelton’s results secured him a place in the ATP Finals for the first time, where he made it out of the group stages before falling to Alcaraz in the semi-finals on Saturday . Making him the youngest American to reach this stage of the tournament since Andy Roddick in 2004

items.title: Coco Gauff admits the main reason why she is happy to be ranked above Jessica Pegula for a fourth year in a row
paras: Coco Gauff has ended the season as the American WTA number one player for a fourth successive year. Gauff has had a mixed 2026 season , having failed to reach a Grand Slam final this year, but won her fourth WTA 1000 title at the Cincinnati Open .

The two-time Grand Slam champion played her most recent tournament at the WTA Finals , where Gauff was eliminated at the round-robin stage. Despite this, Gauff is still the American number one ahead of Jessica Pegula for a fourth consecutive year, as she leads her compatriot by just three ranking points.

Which of these four WTA players will win the most Grand Slams next year? Sabalenka, Gauff and Swiatek all went without a major title in 2026… Gauff beat Pegula at the WTA Finals this year, in a crucial win that has ultimately confirmed her spot as the American number one for a fourth consecutive year.
items.impact: Pegula is the last American other than Gauff to have been the top-ranked player for her nation on the WTA Tour, with former Australian Open champion Sofia Kenin holding this position in both 2020 and 2021.

items.title: Carlos Alcaraz makes comment about Italian tennis fans after reaching the final of the ATP Finals
paras: Carlos Alcaraz defeated Ben Shelton, 3-6, 6-3, 7-6, in the ATP Finals semi-finals. The world number three was in trouble early on, but upped his game to return to the championship match in Turin.

Alcaraz lost to home favourite Jannik Sinner in the final 12 months ago, but with the Italian out of the picture this year, he will fancy his chances of taking the title. During his latest post-match press conference, Alcaraz was asked about the fan support he receives in Italy, and whether he’d noticed it change in 2026, with his biggest rival missing due to injury.

“Well, even when I’m playing against Jannik [Sinner] obviously here in Italy, I just feel it’s not the whole stadium against me, which is, yeah, it’s a step,” said Alcaraz. “But yeah, I feel really loved every time I come here.

items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
